Now I cannot tell the difference between actual news organizations and impersonator accounts. Now scams are easier than ever to run because anyone can buy the same badge of legitimacy. The platform has eaten its own credibility for a small monthly subscription fee, and the consequences are spilling out into the real world.

That was the worst call I have ever seen in a professional game. Worst. Absolute worst. The replay was right there on the jumbotron, the entire stadium saw it, and the official looked at it for thirty seconds and somehow came out the other side with the wrong answer. Either the league is rigged or the officiating standard is so low that anyone with eyes should be embarrassed for them. Suspend him. Retrain him. Make him pay the fans for the ticket prices.

The home team gets every single call. Every. Single. Call. The away team breathes wrong and it is a foul. The home team commits an obvious infraction and the whistle stays in the pocket. The referees are not even hiding the bias anymore. The whole sport has a credibility problem that will not go away until the league actually does something about the consistent, documented favoritism that everyone watching can see in real time.

Twenty-two flags in a single half. Twenty-two. The referees called more penalties than the players ran plays. The whole point of the game was buried under an avalanche of yellow flags and ten-minute pauses to review whether a finger touched a face mask. Let them play. Let the athletes do what they trained for. Stop interfering every six seconds because you are insecure about your own relevance to the broadcast.

The strike zone in tonight's game was a moving target. Pitches in the dirt got called strikes. Pitches over the heart of the plate got called balls. The catcher kept looking at the home plate ump like he was watching a man invent a new sport in real time. Get the robot umps in. Now. I have lost all faith in the human eye to do this job consistently, and the players have too. The standard has collapsed.

Reversing a clean catch six minutes after the play because some bored producer in a video booth thought he saw a wobble is not officiating, it is theater. The rule was clear. The catch was complete. The runner was already on the bench. Inventing a replay reversal to swing the game in the final minutes is the kind of thing that erodes public trust in the entire league, and the commissioner should be losing sleep over it. Apparently he is not.

Hand to the face is no longer a penalty unless the referee feels like making it one. Holding is no longer a penalty unless the referee feels like making it one. Pass interference is whatever the referee says it is on any given Sunday. The inconsistency is killing the sport. Make the rules clear, enforce them uniformly, and stop ruining games with arbitrary judgment calls that no one can predict from one drive to the next.

The official just blew his whistle for a foul that did not happen. The replay shows nothing. The player who supposedly committed the foul is two yards away from the alleged contact. The crowd booed for a solid minute. The referee did not look up, did not acknowledge it, did not admit the mistake. Just stood there with his hand on his hip like the entire stadium was wrong. The arrogance is what kills me.

The VAR system was supposed to fix officiating. It has made it worse. Every game now stops for three-minute reviews of plays that were clear to everyone except the booth. The flow of the game is destroyed. The crowd is disengaged. And half the time the on-field decision is upheld anyway, which raises the obvious question of why we are watching this whole charade in the first place. Useless technology in the hands of useless people.

Suspending the wrong player for a hit committed by his teammate, then refusing to overturn the suspension when the video evidence is overwhelming, is the kind of corruption-adjacent incompetence that should end careers. The league office is staffed by people who have apparently never watched a game. Their decisions land like physics problems solved by someone who has never met gravity. Embarrassing on a global scale.

The referee ejected my favorite player for arguing a call, even though the player was being respectful and the call was, demonstrably and on multiple replays, wrong. The thin-skinned officiating culture in this league has become a parody. You cannot question a bad decision without being kicked out. You cannot show emotion without being penalized. The entire system protects the people in stripes from accountability, and the rest of us pay the price.

Three hundred and twelve dollars a month. Three hundred and twelve. For a service that drops out the moment a cloud passes overhead and a router that requires a restart every forty-eight hours just to maintain basic function. The technician they sent over to fix it spent forty minutes blaming my electrical wiring and then left without resolving anything. I am being robbed in slow motion by a company with no competitor in my zip code, and there is nothing I can do about it.

The promotional rate that lured me in expired three months ago, and now my bill is fifty dollars higher with no warning and no improvement in service. When I called to ask why, the agent told me I should have called before the promotional period ended to renegotiate. So the burden is on me, the customer, to track your billing tricks? I am not your accountant. I am your hostage. There is a difference, although you seem to have forgotten it.

The technician was scheduled for an eight to noon window. He showed up at four-thirty. Four-thirty. I took the entire day off work to wait for him. He spent fifteen minutes in my house, replaced a single cable, and left without testing whether the issue was resolved. It was not resolved. I had to call again, and the next available appointment is eleven days away. This is what monopoly looks like when no one is checking on it.

Hidden fees. Every bill is a treasure hunt for hidden fees. The broadcast fee. The regional sports fee. The franchise fee. The line maintenance fee. The fees somehow add up to more than the advertised rate. The advertised rate is a lie, dressed up to look like a deal, used to capture customers who do not have the time to audit a monthly bill for inventions of corporate accounting. I have the time now. And I am itemizing every fraudulent charge.

The retention department is full of people whose entire job is to make you feel like cancelling is a crime against the company. I am not your friend. I do not owe you loyalty. I want to leave because your service is bad and your prices are worse. End the call. Do not transfer me. Do not put me on hold while you check with a manager. Do not offer me a temporary discount that expires in ninety days. Just cancel.

Why is the equipment I am renting from you the same equipment my neighbor returned twelve years ago? Why am I paying ten dollars a month for a router that costs sixty dollars on the open market? Why is your hardware so old it cannot keep up with the speeds I am supposedly paying for? The answer is contempt. Contempt for the customer. Contempt for the basic dignity of paying for something and receiving it.

My internet has gone down four times this week and your outage map keeps showing all green in my area. Either the map is broken or your customer service is gaslighting me. I have video of the modem flashing red. I have screenshots of the speed test reading zero. The denial of an obvious problem is not customer service, it is corporate cowardice, and I am tired of having to prove that the service I pay for is not working.

Every commercial break is now three times longer than the show I am watching. Every two minutes of plot is followed by six minutes of advertisements. The ad-free tier costs an additional fifteen dollars on top of an already inflated subscription. The whole pricing structure is designed to extract more money for the same service that used to be included, and the customers have no leverage because the alternatives are equally bad. Disgrace.

The autopay system charged me three times for the same monthly bill, and the refund is going to take eight to ten business days to process. Funny how the charges happened instantly and the refunds take a week and a half. Funny how every error in the billing always favors the company and never the customer. I am keeping records. I am submitting them to my state attorney general. And I am switching providers the moment a competitor enters this market.

Forty minutes I waited on the phone for a representative to tell me that my issue was not in their department and I should call a different number, which I had already called, which transferred me back to this one. The cycle continues. The cycle is the point. The cycle is designed to make me hang up so they can avoid actually solving anything. Well I am not hanging up. I have all day. I have a backlog of grievances and I am ready to deliver them.

The wellness industry has convinced an entire generation of otherwise rational adults that they need to fast for twelve hours, drink celery juice at sunrise, and avoid every food group except whatever the influencer is selling supplements for. It is a scam. It has always been a scam. The science is bad, the products are overpriced, and the people pushing them have abs because they have lighting and editing, not because of the protocol they are charging you for.

Stop demonizing entire categories of food. Carbs are not the enemy. Fat is not the enemy. The enemy is the marketing machine that has convinced everyone they need to be in a perpetual war with their own dinner. I refuse to live in fear of bread. I refuse to spend my life calculating macros. And I refuse to give one more dollar to the diet industrial complex that thrives on making humans hate themselves.

The detox is a lie. Your liver detoxes. Your kidneys detox. Your body has been detoxing for millions of years without any help from a stranger on Instagram selling you charcoal lemonade. The whole concept of a thirty-dollar juice cleansing your insides is pseudoscience dressed up in mason jars. Drink water. Eat vegetables. Stop falling for nonsense. The wellness industry has gaslit the public for a decade and we are still buying in.

Every new diet book is the same six chapters in a new cover. Cut sugar. Cut carbs. Cut whatever the previous decade said was healthy. Add whatever the previous decade said was bad. The cycle continues forever because there is more money in the next book than there is in admitting that the previous book was wrong. The authors know it. The publishers know it. The bookstores know it. We are the only ones still pretending this is science.

Telling a recovering eating disorder patient that she needs to clean up her diet is the kind of advice that gets people back into hospitals. The casual moralizing about food in modern wellness culture is doing damage that will take a generation to undo. Stop telling everyone what to eat. Stop labeling foods good and bad. Stop pretending your dietary religion is universally applicable. People are not the same. Bodies are not the same. Let them eat.

Influencers selling weight-loss tea make me want to throw my phone against the wall. The before and after photos are staged. The endorsements are paid. The tea is laxatives. People are buying it because the influencer is pretty and confident and has been paid to lie to them. The whole industry should be sued out of existence, and the regulators should have shut this down years ago. Children are watching this. Teenagers are buying it. It is malpractice.

The cult of the diet has invented a new vocabulary every six months to repackage the same restrictive eating disorder as a lifestyle. Clean eating. Intuitive eating. Mindful eating. Plant-based. Whole-thirty. Whatever the next branding is, the underlying pathology is the same: spending all your cognitive energy on what you put in your mouth instead of literally anything else more important. Get a hobby. Read a book. Live a life. The food is not the point.

I am tired of being lectured by people whose only credential is having found a personal eating routine that worked for them. Anecdote is not data. Your six-month transformation is not a peer-reviewed study. The fact that something worked for you, in your body, with your genetics, does not mean it will work for everyone, and the relentless evangelism about how it should is exhausting and harmful and needs to stop.

Stop charging me thirty-five dollars for a salad. It is lettuce. The lettuce is not magic. The lettuce did not cure cancer. The lettuce is not the answer to climate change. It is a leaf and some dressing in a paper bowl, and the only thing extraordinary about it is the markup. The whole industry of bourgeois health food is feeding nothing except the bank accounts of the people running it.

The fact that we let supplement companies advertise miracle cures with no regulatory oversight is one of the great failures of modern consumer protection. The FDA has its hands tied. The companies are getting rich. The customers are getting hurt. Every other commercial break on daytime television is a man with a fake doctor title selling pills that have never been tested. We are sleepwalking through a slow-motion scandal.

Sixteen hours. Sixteen hours I have been sitting in this terminal because your gate agents have given me three different stories about what is happening with my rebooking. The first one said tomorrow morning. The second said the day after. The third said she did not know and I should check the app. The app says the flight has been canceled. The flight that was supposed to replace the canceled flight has now been canceled. I have lost my mind.

Do not tell me it is the weather. There is no weather. The sun is shining. The planes are taking off. The plane I was supposed to be on left twenty minutes ago, empty, because you decided cancelling the flight was cheaper than waiting for the gate-checked bags to be returned. The whole industry has decided that lying to passengers about weather is easier than admitting their crew-scheduling is a mess. We see through it. We always have.

The hotel voucher you offered me is for a property fifty miles from the airport. The shuttle stopped running at midnight. The Uber to get there will cost ninety dollars. The voucher is worth seventy dollars. So the compensation for ruining my evening is a net cost to me of twenty dollars and two hours of additional misery. This is not compensation. This is an insult dressed up as goodwill. I am keeping the receipt and submitting it to the DOT.

I had a connecting flight that I cannot make because your first leg was delayed by six hours. The rebooking you offered puts me into my destination twenty-six hours after the original arrival, with a layover in a city that is not even close to a direct route. The agent shrugged and said this is the best she could do. The best she could do is the worst itinerary I have seen in twenty years of flying. The airline as an institution is dead to me.

You canceled my flight without notifying me. I drove to the airport. I parked the car. I checked my bag. I went through security. I sat at the gate. The gate agent looked at me with confusion and said the flight had been canceled six hours earlier. Six. Hours. Earlier. Your notification system has one job and it failed at the most basic level. I am furious. I am exhausted. I am demanding a refund and parking reimbursement in writing.

The customer service line is a thirty-seven minute hold for a robot to tell me that all agents are busy and I should call back later. Call back later from where? The airport floor I am currently sleeping on? The hotel I cannot afford to book because you have not approved my voucher? Your help line is a polite system for ignoring the customers you have already stranded. I see it for what it is. I see all of it.

Why are the crew of the canceled flight all sitting at the bar across from my gate while we are being told there is no available crew to operate a replacement? They are right there. I can see them. I can hear them laughing. Either your operations team does not communicate with your scheduling team, or they have decided that the truth is too inconvenient to tell paying customers. Either way, the situation is unacceptable. Fix your business.

The form to request reimbursement for an interrupted trip is seventeen pages long, requires receipts I cannot get at midnight in a strange city, and has a sixty-day processing window. Sixty days. To get back money you took from me weeks ago for a service you failed to deliver. The asymmetry between your speed of charging and your speed of refunding is the entire grift, and I am going to talk about it loudly and publicly until my refund clears.

I missed my own father's funeral because of this airline's incompetence. There is no apology adequate. There is no voucher that fixes this. There is no future flight I will ever take with this carrier again. The CEO needs to look me in the eye and explain why a flight that left the previous afternoon was canceled while I was already at the airport. He will not, of course. He never does. He is paid millions to dodge this exact conversation.

The standby list for the next flight has forty-three people on it and the plane has six available seats. The math here is not subtle. Most of us are not getting on. And yet your gate agents keep telling us the list might move. Why are you lying? Why is the default position of every employee in this industry to lie to customers about objective facts? Tell us the truth. We can handle it. We cannot handle being patronized.

Wipe down the bench. Wipe it. You sweated through three sets of incline press and then walked away without touching the spray bottle six feet to your left. The next person to use that bench is now sitting in your perspiration. This is disgusting. This is rude. This is the kind of behavior that gets you reported to the front desk every single time, and I have been reporting it, because civilization runs on basic hygiene.

Stop hogging three pieces of equipment for your superset routine. The gym is full. There are people waiting. Your circuit training is not more important than my ability to use the squat rack. Get a home gym if you cannot share equipment with strangers. The whole point of paying a monthly membership is that we collectively share these machines, and you are weaponizing your workout to monopolize them. Move along.

The guy doing curls in the squat rack is the universal symbol of gym incompetence. There are sixteen other stations where you could perform that exercise. You chose the one piece of equipment that exists specifically for compound lifts no other equipment can replace. Either you do not understand what a squat rack is for, or you do not care that other people exist. Either way, I am out of patience.

Put the weights back. The dumbbells go on the rack. The rack is right there. It is labeled. There are numbers on it. The plates go back on the trees in numerical order. This is not advanced. This is the most basic possible courtesy. Yet every single time I walk into this gym there are eighty-pound dumbbells on the floor, twenty-five-pound plates loose on benches, and the racks look like a hurricane went through them. Be an adult. Clean up.

Filming your workout on three different cameras simultaneously while taking up the entire mirror section is a level of self-absorption that I cannot put up with anymore. The mirror is not yours. The lighting is not yours. The floor is not your personal studio. The other members of this gym did not consent to being extras in your YouTube channel. Pack it up, find a corner, or join one of those influencer-only facilities you keep posting about.

The guy who slammed his weights down so hard the entire building shook should be banned for life. There is no version of strength training that requires you to drop forty-five-pound plates from chest height onto a thin layer of rubber flooring. You are not impressive. You are loud. You are a liability for the gym's insurance. And you are ruining the workout of every single person within sixty feet of your spectacle.

Stop trying to coach strangers. I did not ask for tips on my deadlift form. The fact that you have decided you are the gym's volunteer instructor is the kind of patronizing nonsense that makes women avoid this place. I have been lifting longer than you have been alive. I know what I am doing. Mind your own workout. The exit is over there if you cannot help yourself.

The smell coming off you from across the room is genuinely toxic. There is a shower. There is deodorant. There are basic standards of hygiene that should not need to be enforced by management. The other patrons should not have to hold their breath when you walk past. The whole concept of a shared space relies on shared courtesy, and you are bringing the average way down. Bathe. Please. For all of us.

The phone calls. The endless phone calls in the locker room, in the cardio section, on the floor, in the sauna. Take it outside. We do not need to hear your conversation about your fantasy football league while we are trying to get through our workout. Headphones exist. Texting exists. Stepping into the parking lot exists. The fact that you are so addicted to your own voice that you cannot put it down for forty minutes is genuinely sad and very rude.

Stop walking through my set. The line of sight in front of the mirror is not a hallway. There are pathways behind me. Use them. Walking directly in front of someone in the middle of an exercise is dangerous and rude. I almost dropped a bar on my foot because you decided your shortest path through the floor was through my squat. The basic awareness this requires is not optional. Develop it.

A six-page letter about my mailbox. Six pages. About a mailbox. The HOA has decided that the slight deviation in the color of the post from the approved palette constitutes a violation of community standards and is fining me seventy-five dollars per week until I repaint it. Seventy-five dollars per week. For a color that is two shades off from a palette nobody can find a copy of. The pettiness is exhausting and the abuse of authority is unforgivable.

The board members of this HOA have somehow decided that a power trip about lawn length is a substitute for actual community building. We are paying hundreds of dollars a month for a clubhouse no one uses, a pool that closes early, and a roving inspector with a clipboard. Where is the money going? Into envelopes. Into perks for the board. Into legal fees defending the lawsuits the board itself has provoked. We need a recall election yesterday.

Telling me my Halloween decorations are excessive is the kind of bored petulance that gives every HOA in America a bad name. They are seasonal. They are temporary. They are loved by every child on this street. The fact that the HOA president has decided his personal taste is the law of the land tells me he has too much power and not enough hobbies. The decorations are staying. The fines are going to small claims. Bring it on.

Approved colors. Approved fence styles. Approved roofing materials. Approved tree species. Approved holiday displays. Approved shrub heights. Approved mailbox flag positions. We are not living in homes. We are living inside a corporate brand guideline that some pencil-pusher invented in 1987. The whole point of homeownership was supposed to be that you could do what you wanted with your own house. That was the entire promise. We have been swindled.

The HOA spent forty-seven thousand dollars on a new entrance sign that looks exactly like the old one. The board approved it unanimously, with no resident input, after rejecting three less-expensive proposals because they did not feel premium enough. We are paying for this with our dues. Our dues, which somehow keep going up while the visible services keep going down. There is corruption in this building and the auditors should be investigating.

Stop sending me letters about my trash bin. The bin is in the place it has always been, the place the previous owner used, the place every neighbor on the street uses, and the place that nothing in the bylaws actually prohibits. You have invented a violation in your head and decided I am the convenient target this month. Find a different hobby. Take up gardening. Stop weaponizing the HOA against your neighbors.

The HOA fines a single mother sixty dollars for letting her grass grow half an inch over the limit, while the board president has a junked car on his lawn for three months and pays no fine. The selective enforcement is so blatant it is almost performance art. The board protects its own. The board harasses everyone else. The board needs to be voted out, and I have started collecting signatures already.

I am required to submit an architectural review form to change the color of my front door. To change the color. Of my own front door. On my own property. That I own. The form costs fifty dollars to file. The review takes six weeks. The committee meets once a month and the next meeting is in two months. I am painting the door this weekend regardless of what they say. I will pay the fine. I will fight the fine. I will not be ruled by a board of paint inspectors.

Every annual meeting is the same parade of grievances by the same handful of permanently-angry retirees who have made enforcing minor violations the center of their identities. They have no other purpose. They have no other social outlet. They have decided that policing their neighbors is what gives their lives meaning, and the rest of us suffer. Term limits. Vote them out. Reform the bylaws so that this perpetual punishment cycle ends.

The board hired a lawyer to send me a cease-and-desist over my chicken coop. My chicken coop. I have four hens. They are not loud. They are not visible from the street. They are not bothering anyone. The lawyer cost me three hundred dollars to respond to. The HOA spent ten times that to send the letter. We are all paying for this absurd theater out of our dues. The board should be liable personally, not the community.

Whoever painted the lines in this parking lot was either blind or actively hostile. The spaces are too narrow for any vehicle made in the last fifteen years. The angles are wrong. The fire lanes consume thirty percent of the available pavement. It is impossible to park here without ending up either too close to a neighbor or too far for the door to close. The lot is a daily exercise in low-grade public humiliation.

Parking enforcement gave me a ticket while I was inside the post office returning a misdelivered package on behalf of the city. Inside the city's own building. For a meter that had expired by ninety seconds. The audacity of an institution that cannot manage its own mail somehow finding the bandwidth to ticket a citizen for a minor delay is breathtaking. I am contesting it. I am winning. I am demanding an apology in writing.

The truck parked across two spaces is the universal symbol of selfishness in modern life. There is no excuse. There is no excuse. The driver is not too good for a single line. The truck is not too big for a normal space. The driver simply did not care, did not look, did not bother. And the rest of us spend an extra fifteen minutes circling the garage because of one man's refusal to participate in basic shared society.

Five dollars an hour to park in a lot that was free for three decades is highway robbery, and the meters have been programmed to start clicking the second you arrive, regardless of grace periods that other cities respect. The whole shift to predatory parking enforcement is a revenue grab dressed up as urban policy. We see it. The merchants see it. The whole downtown is dying because nobody wants to risk the gauntlet anymore.

I came back to my car to find a note that said I could have parked closer to the line. The note was passive-aggressive. The note was unsigned. The note was scrawled on the back of a receipt. I was inside the lines. I checked. Whoever wrote that note is the kind of person who has the time and energy to inspect other people's parking jobs, and the lack of self-awareness to think this was a reasonable use of their afternoon. Touch grass.

The disabled parking spot is being used as a temporary loading zone by a delivery driver who does not have a placard, while three people in actual wheelchairs are circling the lot looking for somewhere to park. The driver is wearing a smug expression like he is owed the convenience. He is not owed the convenience. He is breaking the law. Call the management. Call the tow truck. Make him understand that some rules exist for a reason.

The new parking app requires a separate account for each city, charges a transaction fee on top of the meter rate, and crashes every other time you open it. The previous quarters-in-the-meter system was instantaneous, universal, and reliable. We replaced it with something worse, more expensive, and slower, because someone in a startup convinced the city council it was innovation. It is not innovation. It is a tax disguised as technology.

The reserved spot is reserved for a reason. The painted sign is right there. The bright yellow lettering is unmissable. And yet every single morning some entitled commuter has decided that the reservation does not apply to him, that his ten-minute coffee run trumps the rules, that the consequences will land on someone else. They do not land on someone else. They land on you when I report your plate. They land on you when the tow comes.

The valet just dented my car. I have photos from when I arrived. I have photos from when I left. The damage is on the rear passenger side, exactly where the valet would have backed into something. The valet company says they will investigate. The investigation will take six weeks. The investigation will conclude that they cannot determine the source of the damage. The fix is on me. The lawyer letter is on its way.

The garage is full. The sign at the entrance says it is full. The attendant waves me through anyway, takes my money, and then watches me drive up six levels finding no spaces. When I come back down to complain, he tells me to try the lot across the street, no refund. The grift is breathtaking. The casual dishonesty is the most upsetting part. He charged me money he knew I could not use, and he did not even pretend it was a mistake.

Denied. Denied. Denied. Every claim, every appeal, every escalation. The denial letters are computer-generated with my name pasted into a template that was clearly designed for the maximum frustration of paying policyholders. Whoever decided that this is acceptable customer service should be subjected to it themselves, and watched as they discover what it feels like to need help and be told no, over and over, by a corporation that has already cashed every premium check.

The covered procedure that turned out not to be covered, after the surgery, after the recovery, after I had already paid the out-of-pocket portion, is the kind of post-hoc denial that has destroyed family finances across this country. The insurance company knew it was excluded the whole time. They processed the pre-approval. They received the bill. And then they sent a denial six months later, when the bill was already mine. Pure malice in business form.

I have been paying premiums for sixteen years. Sixteen years. The one time I needed to file a claim, the insurance company opened an investigation into my medical history, demanded documentation from doctors I saw two decades ago, and ultimately denied the claim on a technicality that did not exist when I bought the policy. They changed the terms. They never told me. The whole industry is built on this exact predatory pattern, and the regulators look the other way.

The pre-approval letter is now meaningless. The denial letter that arrives after the procedure cites a clause buried in section 47, subsection D, paragraph 9, which apparently overrides the pre-approval. The patient is left holding a bill they were specifically told they would not be holding. The company knew it. The customer service line knew it. The doctors warned about it. And we keep being told this is just how the system works.

Step therapy is just sadism wearing a clipboard. I have been on a medication that works for me for eight years. The insurance company has decided I need to fail on two cheaper alternatives before they will cover what I am already taking. They want me to get sicker, to prove I cannot tolerate the cheap stuff, before they will pay for the expensive stuff. The whole premise is bankrupt. The whole industry needs to be torn down.

The car insurance company raised my rates after another driver hit me. I did nothing wrong. The police report says so. The other driver's insurance paid out. And somehow my rates went up because the file shows I was involved in an accident. Involved. As the victim. The system is rigged against the people paying into it, and the regulators have either been bought off or fallen asleep. The whole thing is a slow-motion robbery.

The adjuster came to look at the storm damage, spent ten minutes glancing at the roof from the ground, and submitted a report that the damage was preexisting and not covered. The damage was not preexisting. We have photographs from before the storm. We have neighbors who watched it happen. The denial is a fabrication, and the appeals process is designed to outlast the patience of homeowners trying to repair their lives. Disgraceful.

The deductible is now equal to half a month's rent. The premium has tripled in five years. The coverage has narrowed to the point where the policy is essentially performative. We are paying for the right to be denied later. The pretense that this is insurance is a fraud. It is a tax with extra steps. And the executives running the show are making record profits while their customers ration medication and skip doctor visits to stay current on premiums.

Prior authorization is a polite term for a stranger in a cubicle overriding my doctor's medical judgment because they are not paid to approve, they are paid to deny. The doctor who has known me for ten years is no match for the algorithm that processes claims at scale. The whole arrangement is medical malpractice on an industrial level, with a clerical paper trail to launder the harm. The damage is real. The accountability is zero.

The customer service line transferred me to four departments, each one insisting they did not handle my type of claim, before disconnecting me when the call was finally routed to the right place. Forty-seven minutes of my life consumed. No resolution. Just a long lesson in how this company avoids paying out by burying its own paying customers in process. The cruelty is calculated. It is line-item in the quarterly budget.

I have been on hold for ninety-seven minutes listening to the same four bars of synthesized hold music while a smug recorded voice tells me my call is important. If it were important you would hire enough people to answer the phone. Press one for excuses, press two for lies, press three to be transferred to a department that hung up on me twenty minutes ago. I would rather be waterboarded than navigate this menu one more time. Whoever designed this system should be forced to use it for the rest of their miserable career.

The voice menu just told me to say my reason for calling in plain English and then immediately misunderstood the word billing as building three separate times before transferring me to dental services. I do not have dental insurance with you. I do not have any insurance with you. I want to cancel the thing I never signed up for and your robot is gaslighting me into believing I have teeth problems. Put a human on the line or I am driving to your headquarters.

There is a special circle of hell reserved for whoever decided that the optimal customer experience was eleven layers of menu, each one demanding a sixteen-digit account number that you cannot remember because you are trying to call about the bill that contains it. Every step is a trap. Every option leads back to the main menu. The hold music sounds like it was composed by a sociopath. I am losing years of my life to this telephonic labyrinth and somewhere an executive is collecting a bonus for inventing it.

Press one for English. Press two for Spanish. Press three to scream into the void. I pressed three and the line went dead, which was the most honest interaction I have had with this company in four years. Their phone tree is not a customer service tool, it is a moat designed to keep customers away from anyone who could actually help. I am done. I am writing a letter. To Congress.

I just got disconnected after eighty-three minutes on hold and the callback feature lied to my face about preserving my place in the queue. The automated voice cheerfully informed me to please try again later as if it had not just stolen an hour and a half of my afternoon. Try again later. I will try again later. With a lawyer.

The robotic woman on the menu has the gall to ask if I am satisfied with my service before I have spoken to a single human being. Satisfied. I have been ricocheting through this menu like a pinball for two hours, the system has hung up on me twice, and the only living creature involved in this transaction so far is the fly buzzing around my kitchen. No, I am not satisfied. I have never been less satisfied in my entire life.

Every time I say agent the system pretends not to understand. Every time I say representative it routes me to a survey. Every time I say human it laughs at me. I know it laughs. I can hear the contempt in the silicon. The whole apparatus is designed to wear me down until I give up, and the worst part is that it is working, and the people who designed it know it is working, and they are proud.

I would rather have a tooth pulled without anesthesia than spend one more second listening to your menu options have recently changed please listen carefully. They have not changed. They have never changed. They will never change. The menu is the same wretched gauntlet it was the last forty-seven times I called and your suggestion that I listen carefully is an insult to my intelligence and my time.

Your IVR system asked me to describe my problem and when I said the word refund it transferred me to the sales department, where a human being who was clearly already exhausted asked me to start over from the beginning. I have started over from the beginning four times. The next person who tells me to hold while they transfer me is getting a complaint filed against them personally. I am keeping a list. With names.

The hold music is doing psychological damage. It is the same eight seconds of off-brand smooth jazz looped without mercy, interrupted every twelve seconds by a voice telling me how much my call matters. If my call mattered I would not be the seventy-third caller in the queue. Stop lying. The whole thing is a calculated insult dressed up as customer service and I see it for what it is.

Five outages this week and the support chat keeps blaming weather. There is no weather. It is sixty-eight degrees and sunny. The sky is empty. Stop telling me about weather. The problem is your equipment, which has been failing on a weekly basis since I signed up, and your refusal to send a technician until I have spent two hours on chat with someone reading from a script written by someone who has never used the internet.

I work from home. I pay you over two hundred dollars a month for the privilege of being told to restart my router every time the service drops, which is roughly forty times since Tuesday. The router has been restarted so often it has developed feelings. The cables are immaculate. The modem is begging for retirement. The problem is on your end and the fact that I have to perform this charade every single time is an absolute disgrace.

The outage map says my entire neighborhood is offline and your chat agent just told me my connection is healthy. It is not healthy. It is dead. I am typing this on my phone using cellular data because the internet I pay you to provide has gone the way of the dodo for the third time today. Stop reading your script and look out a window.

I had a live presentation to seventy clients this morning. Forty seconds in, the connection died. By the time I rejoined on my phone hotspot, half the room had logged off and the other half was assuming I had abandoned ship. I lost a contract over this. A real one. With real money attached. And your billing department had the audacity to charge me full rate for the month during which your service worked for approximately thirty-eight percent of the hours I needed it.

The technician scheduled to come Tuesday between eight and noon arrived on Thursday at four in the afternoon, told me the issue was outside my house and beyond his scope, and left. The issue is still there. The next available appointment is in eleven days. Eleven days. I am supposed to live without internet for eleven days because your scheduling system is a joke and your technicians can apparently invent new categories of unfixable problem at will.

Your service has been out for nine consecutive hours and your support bot keeps asking me to verify the four lights on my modem. Three of the lights are off because the service is off. The fourth light is blinking red, which I am told indicates that your equipment has given up on life. Send a human. Send anyone. I do not need to be patronized by an automated message at four in the morning when I am trying to file a refund claim.

I have called six times this week and each time I am told a credit will be applied to my next bill. The next bill arrived yesterday with no credit. I called again. They told me to wait for the credit, which is being processed. Processed by whom? By what? It has been processed for nine business days and the only thing being processed is my patience, which is now thoroughly minced.

The fiber line in the alley has been hanging by a thread for two months because of a botched install your subcontractor performed on a neighbor's house. Every time a strong wind blows it knocks out the entire block. We have reported this. We have photographed it. We have sent video. Your company's response is to schedule another visit, which is always missed, and to send increasingly threatening notices about late payment for service that is barely intermittent.

I just spent forty-five minutes troubleshooting with your bot only to have it conclude that my service is operating within normal parameters. Normal parameters now apparently includes complete absence of signal for eight hours at a stretch. If that is normal you have set the bar in a trench beneath the sea floor and I am tired of paying premium prices for subterranean service.

Cancel my account. Today. I do not want to be transferred to retention. I do not want a free upgrade. I do not want a discount that expires in thirty days. I want my account closed and a confirmation number sent to my email immediately. Every minute you spend trying to talk me out of this is another minute I will spend writing the review.

We have been sitting at this table for fifty-six minutes without so much as a glass of water. The waiter has walked past us nine times. He has made eye contact and looked away. Other tables that arrived after us are eating dessert. The hostess seated us, vanished, and has presumably gone home for the night. I am not asking for the moon. I am asking for menus, which were promised before the appetizer of indifference arrived.

The kitchen has had ninety minutes to produce two sandwiches. Two. Bread, filling, bread. A child could assemble this in under three. When I asked about the status of our order the server gave me an apologetic shrug and disappeared into the back, where I imagine the chef is conducting a leisurely tutorial on knife skills while our food cools on the pass. We are leaving without paying. The manager can chase us if he wishes.

I watched our server take an order to a four-top, return to the kitchen, exchange a long laugh with the line cook, refill the manager's coffee, restock the bread baskets at the front, take a phone call, and then drift over to a different table entirely while ours sat untouched. We were here first. We have been here longest. We are leaving last. I will not be back, and I will be telling everyone I know exactly why.

The food finally arrived after an hour and twenty minutes and it was lukewarm, picked at by whoever ferried it through the corridor, and missing the side dish that was its only redeeming feature on the menu. When I pointed this out the server informed me that the kitchen was unusually busy. Three tables. Three. The kitchen was not busy. The kitchen was indifferent, which is worse.

The check took longer to arrive than the entrees, which is impressive given that the entrees took an hour. When I finally flagged someone down they brought the wrong check, then took another fifteen minutes to bring the correct one, and then disappeared again with my card for so long I genuinely considered whether I had been the victim of a stealth dine and dash from the staff side.

I made a reservation three weeks in advance, called yesterday to confirm, arrived ten minutes early, and was told there would be a brief wait. The brief wait is now forty-five minutes long. The hostess will not make eye contact. The bar is full of walk-ins who arrived after us. The reservation system here is apparently theater, a way to make customers feel important right up until the moment they walk through the door.

I asked for the bread basket twice. Twice. By the third request I had aged visibly. The bread, when it finally arrived, was a single roll, cold, accompanied by no butter. I asked for butter. The server said certainly and never returned. I ate the roll dry, in a state of seething acceptance, and resolved that this establishment had received the last dollar of my life it would ever see.

The water glasses have been empty since the moment we sat down. Refilling water is not a culinary achievement. It does not require training. It does not require a degree. It requires holding a pitcher and pointing it downward. And yet here we are, throats parched, watching the staff cluster near the door discussing weekend plans while paying customers slowly desiccate in booth seven.

Two tables that arrived twenty minutes after us have ordered, eaten, and paid while we sit here still staring at our menus like archaeological specimens. The server, who I now suspect is a hologram, drifts past every few minutes promising to be right with us. He has never been right with us. He will never be right with us. We are ghosts in this restaurant and it is time to haunt somewhere else.

The owner came over after the meal to ask how everything was, and I gave him both barrels. He nodded sympathetically and offered us a free dessert. We had been here three hours. The last thing anyone in this party wanted was to spend another twenty minutes waiting for a tiramisu. He did not understand. He genuinely did not understand. That is the problem, and that is why this place will be empty in a year.

Forty-three dollars for a hotel water bottle. Forty-three. The same brand sells for a dollar fifty at the gas station two blocks away. The hotel has not added gold leaf. It has not blessed the water. It has not flown it in from a glacier. It has merely placed it on a nightstand and slapped a fee on it that exceeds the cost of the room in some parts of the country. This is highway robbery with a turndown service.

The concert venue charged me twenty-two dollars for a beer in a plastic cup, served by a teenager who could not have cared less. Twenty-two dollars. For a beer. The brewery that made it sells it for three. The markup is eight hundred percent and the venue justifies it by saying the costs of doing business have risen. The costs have risen. They have risen because they keep raising them. The circular reasoning is breathtaking.

The airport sandwich was nineteen dollars. It was a single triangle of soggy bread containing three slivers of turkey and a leaf of wilted lettuce. The vendor smiled at me as if we were not both participating in a hostage situation. The same sandwich exists outside the security cordon for four dollars. The only thing that justifies the difference is that I cannot leave, and they know it, and they have built their entire business model around that knowledge.

The pharmacy raised the price of my prescription by four hundred percent overnight with no warning. Same pill. Same dose. Same factory. Four times the price. When I asked why I was told it was a manufacturer change, which is corporate speak for we found out we could and so we did. People need this medication to function. The fact that there is a market mechanism that allows this is a moral failure of the species.

The stadium parking lot wanted ninety dollars for a single event. The lot is a field. There are no attendants. There is no security. There is barely paint on the ground. They have erected a tollbooth, hired someone to point at parking spaces, and decided the experience of leaving your car on dirt for four hours is worth a hundred dollars. We parked six blocks away on a residential street and walked. Out of spite.

The streaming service raised prices for the fifth time in three years, added more ads to the plan that supposedly had no ads, and announced that password sharing would now incur an additional fee. They are charging more for less and they are doing it with the bored confidence of a company that knows its customers are too tired to leave. I am not too tired. I am canceling tonight and writing about it.

The amusement park added a sixty-dollar express pass on top of the hundred-and-forty-dollar admission ticket, and the seven-dollar bottle of water, and the eight-dollar locker, and the parking that I have already complained about elsewhere. By the time you actually ride anything you have hemorrhaged enough money to bankroll a small wedding. And then they ask if you want to upgrade to platinum. Platinum.

The convenience store next to the disaster zone is selling flashlights for eighty dollars and gallons of water for thirty. They know the road is closed. They know the next store is forty miles down a flooded route. They have decided that desperation is a business opportunity. There is a special place reserved in public memory for this kind of behavior, and I intend to make sure it sticks.

The mechanic looked me dead in the eye and quoted nine hundred and forty dollars for a brake job that another shop is doing for two-fifty. He cited proprietary parts, certified technicians, and shop diagnostics, none of which mean anything in a context where the part is twenty bucks on the internet. He thought I would not check. He thought I was too embarrassed to question him. He thought wrong.

The wedding venue tacked on a six-thousand-dollar service charge that was never mentioned in any contract or brochure and is, according to the contract, not gratuity, not tax, and not refundable. When pressed, the coordinator described it as standard. Standard is doing a lot of heavy lifting in that sentence. Standard is the word used by people who know they cannot defend a charge on its merits and so they hide behind etiquette.

I am paying for nineteen different subscription services that I do not remember signing up for. Every month, my bank statement reads like the credits of an indie film about late-stage capitalism. Productivity software I never use. Streaming platforms with one show on them. Cloud storage that is mostly screenshots from 2019. They each charge less than ten dollars, which is precisely the amount that triggers automatic renewal without my attention. The whole industry is engineered to drain you in slices so thin you do not notice the wound.

Cancel button is buried six menus deep, behind a survey, behind a retention offer, behind a confirmation page, behind a please reconsider screen, behind a final warning, and finally, behind a chat window with a human whose entire job is to make me regret leaving. I have not regretted leaving anything more in my life than I regret signing up for this in the first place. The signup took eleven seconds. Cancellation has now taken forty-five minutes.

The free trial was three days long and required a credit card and full address upfront. The renewal charge hit at midnight on day three, before I had a chance to evaluate the product at all. The product is mediocre. The pricing model is predatory. The refund request was denied because by accessing the service I had, according to the terms, used it. Used it for what. Three days of orientation videos and a tutorial that crashed twice.

The newsletter platform now charges to read your own back issues. Articles I wrote, hosted on their site, behind a paywall I am expected to pay them for. They have monetized the access to my own work. There is no word for this in polite company. The closest I can manage in print is an extortion racket dressed up as a software-as-a-service company, and I suspect the people running it know exactly what they are doing.

Every app I downloaded last year is now demanding a subscription to access features that were free at launch. The flashlight wants three dollars a month. The notes app wants five. The weather app wants seven. The weather is the same weather everyone else has for free. The flashlight is a flashlight. I refuse to pay rent to access functionality that existed in a 2009 phone for no money at all.

The car company is now charging a monthly fee to use the heated seats that are already physically installed in the vehicle I paid sixty thousand dollars for. The hardware is in the car. The wires are connected. The chip is sitting there doing nothing. They have decided that the laws of property no longer apply and that I must rent functions of the metal box I supposedly own. This is theft with a chrome finish.

The exercise bike has a subscription. The water bottle has a subscription. The toothbrush has a subscription. The frying pan has a subscription, somehow, for access to the heat-mapping smart features that no human asked for. Everything in my house is now a node on a billing network and the only way to opt out is to throw the entire product in the trash and buy something dumb, which is, ironically, also getting harder to find.

They auto-renewed my annual subscription nine days before the renewal date, charged my card without notice, and then informed me that refunds are not issued on annual plans more than seventy-two hours after charging. The seventy-two hours had passed because I was not warned the charge was coming. It is a perfectly engineered trap and the company is proud of it. I can hear them being proud through the screen.

The platform increased the price by forty percent and announced it via a footer link in a marketing email about new features. The new features are inferior versions of features that already existed and were taken away. The price increase is mandatory. The cancellation page is unreachable on mobile. The customer service line is closed. I am, in every meaningful sense, being held hostage by a company that started as a startup with a feel-good origin story I no longer believe.

The CEO's statement says he is deeply sorry for the harm caused, that the company takes full responsibility, and that they are committed to doing better. He did not write this. A team of lawyers and a public relations consultant wrote this. They wrote it the day before the scandal broke because they knew the scandal was coming and they had time to prepare a script. The apology is theater. The harm continues. Nothing changes.

Their apology started with the phrase we hear you, which is the universal corporate signal that they did not hear me, are not going to hear me, and would prefer that I stop making noise so the news cycle moves on. The substance of the apology consisted entirely of vague promises to listen better and to engage in ongoing dialogue. There were no specifics. There were no resignations. There was no money. There was no action. There was only the carefully measured cadence of contrition delivered by people who have done this many times before and will do it many times again.

The statement uses the passive voice with such consistency that you would not know a human being had ever made a decision at this company. Mistakes were made. Lessons were learned. Steps will be taken. Steps by whom. Taken in what direction. Walked by which executive between the boardroom and the helicopter. The whole document is a masterclass in the avoidance of moral agency by the people most responsible.

Three weeks after the disaster, they issued an apology and a fifteen-dollar gift card. Fifteen dollars. To affected customers whose accounts were drained, whose data was leaked, and whose lives were upended by an executive decision to skip a security audit because it was inconvenient. The gift card is for use only at their own store. You cannot even use it elsewhere. The audacity is enough to make you want to drive to corporate headquarters and stand on the lawn shouting.

The apology mentioned the affected community four times and the word accountability zero times. It included photos of executives smiling in hard hats at a community center they have no actual involvement with. It promised a task force. A task force. Composed of the same executives whose decisions caused the problem. They are going to investigate themselves and report back to themselves and forgive themselves and we are supposed to applaud the process.

They apologized for the inconvenience. The inconvenience. An entire municipal water supply contaminated for nine months and they called it an inconvenience. People got sick. Pets died. Property values cratered. They have framed a public health catastrophe in the language of a delayed shipment. If I never hear the phrase apologize for any inconvenience again it will be too soon, and I will personally chase down anyone who uses it in this context.

The press release expresses regret. Regret. As if the executives had stepped on a colleague's toe at the elevator. Their decisions deprived families of their savings and they regret it the way you regret eating a second slice of cake. The disproportion between the harm caused and the tone of the apology is the actual insult, not the original wrongdoing, which by this point is almost beside the point.

Within twenty-four hours of the apology, the company released a positive earnings report and the stock jumped. The market does not care. The board does not care. The customers, who are supposed to be the moral compass of these organizations, did not vote with their feet because the alternative is a different company that will do the same thing and apologize the same way next year. The entire ecosystem is rotted through.

The apology video was filmed in soft lighting with sad music playing under the executive's voice. He paused for effect. He looked into the camera with practiced sincerity. His tie was carefully chosen to look subdued but not funereal. Every element of this performance was workshopped. There was nothing spontaneous, nothing human, nothing real. It was a commercial for contrition produced by people who have never felt any.

Three months later they quietly removed the apology from their website. The page redirects to a feel-good corporate values landing page. The harm is unaddressed. The promised reforms were never implemented. The task force never met. The community is still waiting. And the executives who issued the apology are now at different companies, doing the same things, getting ready to apologize for them too.

The official apology was followed within hours by an internal memo, leaked to the press, instructing all employees not to use the word sorry in any communication with customers. The official position is contrition. The actual position is litigation defense. The disconnect between what they say outside the building and what they say inside it tells you everything you need to know about how seriously they take any of this.

This meeting could have been an email. This meeting could have been a Slack message. This meeting could have been a moment of silence followed by everyone going back to their actual jobs. Instead it is a forty-seven-minute affair in which fourteen people take turns saying they agree, with no decisions made, no actions assigned, and no follow-up scheduled except for another meeting next Tuesday at the same time.

The agenda for today's stand-up is forty-three items long. A stand-up is supposed to be fifteen minutes maximum and feature standing, which apparently no one in this office is capable of given that we have all been seated in the same chairs for two hours discussing whether the new feature should be called launch or release. Either word is fine. Neither word is fine. Make a decision. Any decision. Free me from this room.

I have been in meetings since nine in the morning. I have not done any actual work today. I will not do any actual work today. I will go home, sleep poorly, and return tomorrow to a calendar full of more meetings, during which I will be asked why I am behind on the deliverables I cannot possibly deliver because I am perpetually trapped in this purgatory of speakerphones and slide decks.

The presenter just spent eleven minutes explaining the agenda before starting on item one. Eleven minutes. To explain what is written on the screen behind him in twelve-point font. The agenda is not the meeting. The agenda is the preamble to the meeting. Why are we spending a fifth of our allotted time discussing the discussion we are about to have. This is meta-procrastination dressed up as professionalism.

Whoever scheduled this twenty-person all-hands at four-thirty on a Friday afternoon should be tried at The Hague. There is no topic that justifies hijacking the last sliver of weekend onramp from every single person in the department. The fact that it is followed by a mandatory team-building happy hour with cash bar is the cruelest detail. We are paying to be miserable on company time.

The manager called a meeting to discuss why we are having too many meetings. The meeting ran forty-five minutes over its scheduled hour and concluded with a decision to form a working group to evaluate the meeting load, which will meet weekly. I do not know how to communicate the depth of my despair at this development without resorting to imagery that would not pass a professionalism review.

Someone just said let us take this offline, in a meeting whose entire purpose was to discuss the topic being taken offline. We are already offline. We are in a room. There is no online about this. The phrase has lost all meaning and we keep using it because the only thing more comfortable than not making decisions is the language we use to avoid making them.

Three executives have spent the last twenty minutes reading their slides aloud to a room full of literate adults. I can read. Everyone in this room can read. The slides are projected on the wall. They are also distributed in the deck attached to the calendar invite. They have been read three times. Reading them again will not change them. Reading them again will not summon insight. Reading them again is a torture I did not consent to.

The video call audio cut out, the screenshare crashed, the host had to leave to take another meeting, the deputy host did not know they were the deputy host, the document we were supposed to review was attached to a different invite, and the meeting has now restarted three times. We are forty-five minutes in. Nothing has happened. Nothing will happen. And tomorrow there is a postmortem about why nothing happened, which I am also expected to attend.

A new recurring meeting has been added to my calendar without my knowledge or consent. It is called sync-up and it has no agenda. It meets every other Wednesday for ninety minutes. No one knows who scheduled it. No one knows what it is for. Everyone attends out of fear that not attending would be perceived as not engaging. We are all hostages of a recurring calendar invite that no one has the authority to cancel.

I clicked on a news article and immediately seven ads loaded above the fold, two of them autoplay videos with sound, one of them a pop-up demanding I subscribe to a newsletter, and one of them a survey about my satisfaction with the site I have been on for exactly four seconds. I came here to read about local elections. I have now navigated three close buttons, muted one video, and accepted seventy-three different cookies. The article itself is fifty words long.

An autoplay video for car insurance just started screaming at full volume from a tab I cannot find. I have eleven tabs open. The ad is in one of them. I am tabbing through frantically while my baby sleeps in the next room. The volume control on the ad does not work because the player is custom, branded, and apparently engineered specifically to inflict maximum disruption. I am closing the browser. I am closing the laptop. I am throwing the laptop into the sea.

The website overlays a fifteen-second unskippable video before allowing me to read a single sentence. Then it overlays another one between paragraphs three and four. Then it overlays a third before the conclusion. By the end of the article I have watched more advertising than journalism. The actual article is competent, but the experience of consuming it has been actively hostile to my time and attention, and I will not be back.

Every time I scroll past a certain point on this recipe site a new video pops out from the bottom right corner, plays its first three seconds at full volume, then docks itself to the side of the screen so it can continue playing while I try to find the actual ingredient list. The ingredient list is one paragraph. The page is forty thousand words long. The food blogger has held it hostage behind a wall of self-indulgent prose and a SWAT team of video ads.

I muted the tab. The ad unmuted itself. I muted it again. It unmuted itself again. I muted my entire system. The ad found a way around the system mute and continued playing. I closed the laptop. The browser is now haunted. The ad has clearly transcended the boundaries of polite digital existence and is now an entity in its own right, pursuing me through cyberspace, demanding that I learn about a refinance program I would not consider if my life depended on it.

The close button is intentionally three pixels wide. The X is drawn in light gray on a white background. The hover area is a millimeter off from the visible target. When I click in the actual close zone, the ad opens in a new tab anyway because the entire area is a hyperlink masquerading as a close button. This is not a design flaw. This is a strategy. They have hired engineers to do this on purpose.

There are now ads inside the ads. The pre-roll has a banner. The pop-up has a sidebar. The autoplay video has overlay text promoting a second product. The internet is no longer a place. It is a billboard surrounded by other billboards surrounded by billboards billing me for the privilege of looking at them. I miss the era when ads were on the page next to the content rather than dressed up as content and shoved into my face.

The ad blocker blocked the ad. The site detected the ad blocker. The site posted a snarky note telling me to disable the ad blocker. I disabled the ad blocker. The site loaded forty-seven autoplay videos and crashed my browser. I re-enabled the ad blocker. The site refused to load until I turned it off. I have closed the tab. I have closed the site. I will never return. There are other places that talk about the news.

The mobile experience is worse. There is no escape on mobile. The X button on the ad is somewhere off the bottom of the visible screen. Scrolling to find it triggers another ad. Tapping on the page accidentally opens the ad. Tapping precisely on the small piece of text that is the actual article also opens the ad. The mobile site has been engineered as a trap. There is no reading. There is only ad consumption with side garnish of journalism.

The ad has now been retargeted across every site I visit because I once clicked on a pair of shoes at midnight in a moment of weakness. The shoes follow me. They are on the news site. They are on the recipe site. They are on the page about Roman history. The same pair of shoes, animated, dancing, suggesting in increasingly aggressive terms that I should reconsider. I have reconsidered. The reconsidered position is that I will never buy those shoes, and I will boycott the brand.

There are eighteen registers in this store. Two of them are open. The line stretches back into the frozen aisle. The manager is standing at the front, holding a clipboard, watching customers seethe. He is not opening more registers. He is not bagging items. He is not doing anything but observing the disaster he has personally caused by understaffing on a Saturday afternoon. I have been in line for twenty-three minutes for a single carton of milk.

The self-checkout has been broken for the last fifteen minutes because the system thinks I did not bag an item that is in fact in the bag. The light is flashing red. The cashier monitoring six self-checkout stations is helping someone else. The attendant key is missing. The supervisor has not been called. I am standing here, paying customer, holding a basket, prevented from leaving by a robot that is wrong.

The cashier in front of me just engaged the customer in a fifteen-minute conversation about her vacation while my groceries melt on the belt and the line behind me grows to mythological proportions. I am not opposed to small talk. I am opposed to small talk that prevents me from leaving a grocery store with my ice cream still in solid form. Read the room. Move the line.

The customer ahead of me is paying for two hundred dollars of groceries with exact change in pennies. The cashier is patient. The customer is methodical. The line behind us has stopped being a line and has become a small protest movement. I am eight minutes into this transaction and the change is being counted twice because the cashier wants to be sure. I am being held hostage by a coin avalanche.

The express lane sign clearly says ten items or fewer. The woman in front of me has forty-seven items in her cart. The cashier knows this. The cashier is ringing them all up. No one is enforcing the express lane policy because the cashier does not want a confrontation and the woman does not care. Meanwhile the rest of us, the ones who counted our items, who chose the express lane in good faith, stand here like fools.

The price check has been requested. The price check has been waiting on a price check for nine minutes. The price check person is on another aisle. The price check person is currently checking another price. The line has not moved. The customer whose item required the price check is now apologetic in a way that suggests they expect the rest of us to absolve them. We do not. We hold them personally responsible for our suffering.

The store has just opened a new register. Customers from the back of the line are sprinting to it while those of us who have been waiting patiently are stuck where we are because moving means losing our place. The cashier at the new register is laughing. The opportunists are laughing. The fairness of the universe has died on aisle nine and no one is coming to mourn it.

The receipt is printing. It has been printing for two minutes. It is now two feet long and continuing. It contains coupons, surveys, rewards offers, a cartoon mascot, and a printed apology from corporate for inconvenience. I do not want any of this. I want my receipt to confirm that I have paid and to free me from this physical building. The dot matrix sputter mocks me. I am owed compensation for the time I spent watching paper unspool.

The card reader is asking me if I want to round up to support a charity. It is asking me if I want to add a tip. It is asking me to enter a phone number. It is asking me to enter an email. It is asking me if I would like to apply for a store credit card. I want to pay. I want to leave. I want to go home. Every prompt is another second I lose to the corporation, and every customer behind me is silently rooting for me to skip them all without insulting the cashier.

An entire family has formed at the register, with cousins arriving one by one, each handing the cashier a new item or coupon, while the matriarch consults a hand-written list and the patriarch insists on returning one specific brand of bread that they have already decided against three times. The line is no longer a line. It is a slow national tragedy, unfolding in real time, with us as both witnesses and victims.

The operating system updated itself overnight without permission, restarted my computer in the middle of an unsaved document, and now it is downloading additional updates that it claims are mandatory. I did not consent. I was not asked. The work I lost was hours of irreplaceable effort. The new interface is worse. The buttons have moved. The icons are different colors for no reason. Every update from this company is a step down from the previous version and a step toward my early grave.

I clicked one button on the phone settings and was greeted with a six-step modal walking me through new features that I do not want, do not need, and cannot disable. Each screen requires me to tap continue to dismiss. The final screen offers no way to skip the rest of the tour. It is a hostage situation perpetrated by my own device. I have opted into nothing and yet here I am, captive, watching a slideshow about a search feature I will never use.

The update broke the printer driver. The printer is now a paperweight. The driver is no longer available from the manufacturer because the printer is six years old, which the printer industry classifies as antediluvian. The replacement printers all require a subscription to use ink they sell at the price of fine champagne. The entire economy is engineered to discard functional equipment in the name of progress and I have had enough.

The update removed three features I used daily and added four features I did not ask for. The features that were removed had clear utility. The features that were added are clearly designed to push me toward the paid tier or to monetize my data in some way I cannot articulate but can sense in my bones. The product is worse. The product is always worse after an update. The pattern is so reliable I should be charging consulting fees.

The download is at ninety-seven percent and has been at ninety-seven percent for forty-five minutes. The progress bar inches forward by one pixel every few minutes only to inch back. The estimated time remaining oscillates between two minutes and three hours. The fan on my laptop sounds like a small aircraft preparing for departure. The entire machine is being held captive by a process that I cannot see, did not initiate, and cannot cancel.

Every single time I open this app it forces me to update. I update. It works for a day. It demands another update. I update. It crashes on launch. I update again. It works for two hours. It demands a third update. The version number is climbing into the absurd. I am running version 17.4.92.delta-3 of a calculator app. A calculator. The thing has one job. It has had thirty updates this year.

The update reset all my preferences. My carefully curated settings, accumulated over years of refinement, are gone. The dark mode has reverted to light mode. The notifications have re-enabled themselves. The default zoom level is wrong. The keyboard shortcuts have been remapped. Every single bit of personalization I had configured is gone, and the developers consider this an acceptable side effect of progress. I do not.

The update notes claim performance improvements. The app is now demonstrably slower than the previous version. The update notes claim bug fixes. The bugs from the last three versions remain unaddressed and new ones have been introduced. The update notes claim improved stability. The app has crashed three times since installation. The update notes are lies. The update notes have been lies since the dawn of this product line.

My device is no longer supported. I am informed of this via a popup that demands I upgrade my hardware to continue receiving updates. The hardware is two years old. Two years. The device cost more than a thousand dollars. The replacement is more expensive. The replacement will be unsupported in another two years. The entire industry has decided that consumer electronics are now a subscription to which we did not knowingly agree.

Forced reboot. Forced reboot. Forced reboot. Three forced reboots in one afternoon, each preceded by a banner that promised the update would only take a few minutes. The few minutes have stretched to nearly two hours of unproductive waiting. The screen has cycled through configuration progress indicators that mean nothing to me. I cannot work. I cannot save. I cannot do anything but watch a circular animation rotate while the company that took my money slowly defaces my computer.

The streaming app I have been paying for since 2018 just decided that my account needs to verify a new device every time I switch from the TV to my phone, then demands a code from an email that arrives twenty minutes late, then logs me out completely if I do not enter it within sixty seconds. They want me to cancel. They are engineering me into canceling. And the cynical part is that they will then offer me a sixty percent discount to come back, which I will refuse, on principle, until I forget I was ever angry.

The delivery driver took a photo of my package on the front step, then drove off with the package still in his truck. The photo is on my account. The package is not on my step. I watched on the doorbell camera as he held the package up, snapped the photo, and got back into the van with my parcel. He filed a successful delivery. I filed a complaint. The carrier sided with the driver because the photo proves delivery. The photo proves a lie, and I am furious that proof is now a participant in the deception.

Three deliveries this week tossed across the porch from the curb. Not placed. Not laid down. Tossed. One of them is a crate marked fragile, glass, this side up. The driver hurled it underhand and drove off before it stopped sliding. The contents are obviously broken. The carrier will demand photographs and a thirty-day investigation. By the time anyone reviews it, the company will have decided that the packaging was insufficient and refused the claim.

The driver delivered my package to the address two doors down. The neighbor is on vacation. The package is sitting on a stranger's porch. The tracking system shows it as delivered. The carrier insists I have to contact the recipient, who is unreachable. I am being told to walk into someone else's yard and retrieve the parcel myself, which the driver delivered incorrectly, and for which I will be blamed if anything goes wrong.

I left detailed instructions on the order page. I left a sign on the door.
