I texted the driver through the app. The package was nonetheless left in the rain in the worst possible spot, on a part of the porch with no overhang, six feet from the dry covered porch space clearly indicated by the sign and instructions. The contents were ruined. The driver claims he did not see the instructions. He did not look. He did not care. He did not want to.

The doorbell camera caught the driver kicking my package into the bushes because it would not balance on the railing. He then took a photo, presumably of the bush, and called it delivered. I had to crawl through the hedge in business clothes to retrieve my own package. The shrubbery has scratched the box. The contents have shifted. I will be filing a complaint, a chargeback, and an unkind review with a still frame from the doorbell as the cover image.

The driver rang the doorbell, waited zero seconds, and left a note saying no one was home. I was home. I was walking down the stairs. I opened the door three seconds after the bell rang. The van was already pulling out of the driveway. The note instructs me to drive eleven miles to a depot to pick up my own package, between hours that do not align with my work schedule, by Friday, or the package will be returned. This is not delivery. This is dropping off a homework assignment.

He drove over the lawn. The lawn now has two deep tire ruts where the grass used to be. The driveway was clear. There was no obstruction. He chose, deliberately, to take a shortcut through landscaping I have spent two summers cultivating. When I called the company, they said the driver denies any contact with the lawn. The doorbell video shows the tires, the lawn, and the trajectory. Denial is the only tool they have left.

The package was marked delivered at 3:47 PM. At 3:47 PM I was standing on the porch, on the phone with my mother, watching the empty driveway. No truck came. No driver appeared. The package was not delivered to my address. It was delivered to someone else, or to no one, or to the back of the truck where it remains, while the tracking system invents a fiction in which my package is in my hands.

The driver knocked once, very softly, while standing twelve feet from the door. He did not ring the bell. He did not call out. He left within four seconds of the knock, and the package, which required a signature, has now been returned to the depot. To get my own package, I will need to take a day off work, drive to a distant warehouse, prove my identity, and personally retrieve the item that was supposed to be delivered to my front door.

The status update says the address was not accessible. The address has been accessible to every other delivery driver who has visited it in fifteen years. The address is on a paved street with clear signage and a numbered mailbox. The driver simply did not feel like making the stop. He marked it inaccessible and moved on. The carrier will defend this judgment for as long as it takes me to give up.

Three packages were stacked on top of each other in front of the door, blocking the door from opening. I had to climb out the side window to retrieve them. The driver knew the door opened outward. He had been here before. He chose this configuration as a kind of malicious art installation. I am tempted to leave a thank-you note that he will find genuinely confusing.

Sixteen pieces of junk mail today. Sixteen. The mailbox cannot close. The envelopes are addressed to past residents, to current residents, to occupants in general, and to one person who has been dead for eleven years. The advertisements are for products no one has ever asked for. The political flyers are for elections in districts I do not live in. The catalogs are for stores that have not existed in a decade. The mail system has become a vector for delivering garbage and the postal service is complicit.

I have requested removal from this mailing list six times. Six. Each time the company assures me that it can take up to ninety days for the change to take effect. Ninety days has elapsed five times. The mail keeps coming. The mail will always keep coming. The opt-out is a fiction, a soothing lie that the company tells customers so they feel like they have done something. They have done nothing. I have done nothing. The mail wins.

The credit card offer arrived in an envelope marked URGENT in red, with FINAL NOTICE printed across the front, and a fake check inside that looks like real currency to a confused parent or grandparent. The whole thing is engineered to deceive. There is nothing urgent. There is no final notice. There is no money. There is only a predatory financial instrument dressed up as something else, mailed to my house, addressed to me by name, and entirely legal somehow.

The political mailer is a glossy oversized postcard featuring an unflattering photograph of a candidate I have never heard of, accusing them of crimes that did not occur, in a font that is hard to read by design. The bottom of the card lists the funding source as a PAC with a vaguely patriotic name that nobody has ever investigated. I will throw this away. I will throw away eleven more like it. The forests cleared for this nonsense will haunt our descendants.

The roofing company has sent me a flyer every week for the last fourteen months. I do not need a new roof. I do not own a house that needs a new roof. I rent. The roof is the landlord's problem. The roofing company does not care. The roofing company is operating on a strategy of attrition, hoping that eventually my roof will need replacing and I will be too worn down to choose a different company. They have miscalculated. I will choose any other company purely out of spite.

The catalog is two hundred pages long. Two hundred. Glossy, full color, mailed in shrink wrap. It advertises products that are also available on a website where any reasonable customer would find them faster. The catalog is environmentally indefensible, financially questionable, and culturally archaic. It exists because someone in marketing has convinced the company that catalog recipients spend more money, and that piece of folklore is enough to keep killing trees forever.

Every mortgage refinance company in a hundred-mile radius now has my address. They have all sent me identical letters this month. They have all printed my name in a slightly off shade of black that looks fraudulent on purpose. They all reference my current loan in a way designed to alarm me. None of them have ever spoken to me. None of them know my financial situation. They are spamming the mailbox of every homeowner in the zip code and counting on a fraction of one percent biting.

The insurance solicitation arrived in a window envelope designed to look exactly like a government document. The return address contains a string of letters meant to evoke an official agency. The contents are entirely commercial. The targeting is grandparents and elderly people who are still trained to take mail seriously. The whole industry of dressing up sales pitches as official correspondence should be illegal and is not, because the people who would make it illegal are also benefiting from the practice in ways no one will admit.

The shredder is full of junk mail. The recycling bin is full of junk mail. The trash is full of junk mail. I spend twenty minutes a week processing paper that exists only to advertise products I will never buy. The mailroom is a one-way pipe of corporate effluent flowing into my home and I have no faucet to close.

The supermarket flyer arrived crumpled, soaking wet, half illegible, and advertising prices that expired three days ago. The chain has spent money to manufacture, print, distribute, and deliver this object, all of which I will spend three seconds removing from my mailbox and depositing into the bin. The transaction has cost them several cents and me an entire moment of my limited life on this planet. Multiply this by every household in the country.

The realtor's postcard claims my house is in high demand and that a buyer is currently looking in my neighborhood. There is no buyer. There is never a buyer. The same postcard, with minor variations, has arrived every month for three years. The realtor's smiling face is laminated onto a refrigerator magnet glued to the card. I have peeled off the magnet. I have used it to hold up grocery lists. The realtor has involuntarily contributed something useful to my household for the first time.

The form has rejected my phone number seven times. The form wants the phone number in a specific format. The form will not tell me what the format is. I have tried with dashes, without dashes, with parentheses, without parentheses, with a country code, with spaces, without spaces. Each time the form blanks the entire field and asks me to start over. I have lost three other fields of data in the process. I am ready to find the developer and have a discussion.

The session timed out. The form is gone. The data I entered, over the course of forty-three minutes, painstakingly, with documents pulled from filing cabinets across the house, is gone. The timeout warning gave me ten seconds to respond, hidden in a popup behind the main window where I could not see it. The form must be re-completed in full. There is no draft mode. There is no save. The platform was designed by people who hate human beings.

The form will not accept my address because the apartment number field is required, even though I do not live in an apartment. I have entered N/A. I have entered None. I have entered zero. I have entered the word house. The form rejects all of them. The dropdown for apartment number contains only floors of buildings the form thinks I might live in. I am not in any of those buildings. The form does not believe me.

The CAPTCHA has asked me to identify crosswalks fourteen times. I have identified them fourteen times. It does not believe me. I am clearly a human. I am clearly the kind of human who is increasingly furious with the platform that demands I prove my humanity at every turn. The robot detector is broken. The site has decided that I am suspicious. The site will not let me complete the task I came here to do. The site has won, by attrition, and I have lost, by being a person.

The error message says please correct the highlighted fields. There are no highlighted fields. Every field looks the same. The error message is referring to something I cannot see. The submit button is grayed out. The page does not scroll to the offending field. The form has decided to be cryptic for sport. There is no help text, no tooltip, no clarifying language. I am supposed to guess. I refuse to guess. I have closed the tab and abandoned the application entirely.

The PDF form was downloaded, filled out, printed, signed, scanned, and uploaded back to the same site, where it was rejected because I did not use the latest version of the PDF, which is dated yesterday. The form was identical yesterday. The form is identical today. The version number has changed. The version number is the only thing that has changed. The institution has invented bureaucracy as performance art and I am the unpaid actor.

The form will not let me proceed because my password contains a special character. It then refuses to let me proceed without a special character. The two rules are mutually exclusive. There is no combination of characters that satisfies the validation logic. I have tried for twenty minutes. I have invented passwords of increasing eccentricity. The system has rejected all of them. I am locked out of an account I created today, by rules that contradict themselves, on a platform that does not respond to support requests.

The form has asked me three times to confirm that I am the person filling out the form. I have confirmed three times. The form remains skeptical. The form has now sent a code to my phone, which I have entered. The form has sent a code to my email, which I have entered. The form has now asked me to upload a photo of my driver's license, which I have done. The form has now asked me to take a selfie. I am not applying for a security clearance. I am ordering replacement filters for a refrigerator.

The save button is at the top of the form. The submit button is at the bottom of the form. The form does not save automatically. If you forget to save before clicking submit, the form fails validation, takes you back to the top, and discards everything below your save point. I have lost an hour of work to this design choice. The developer responsible has, I assume, never used a form in their life.

The application requires a notarized document, three forms of identification, two utility bills, a fingerprint card, and a personal essay explaining why I want the thing I am applying for. The thing I am applying for is a library card. The application has somehow expanded to require more verification than a passport. The librarian inside the building has the authority to bypass all of this. The website does not.

Six guys are sitting on the bench press taking turns at a leisurely pace and chatting about supplements between sets. They are using the bench. They are not using the bench. They are leaning against it. They are scrolling on their phones near it. They have effectively claimed the bench as their hangout zone. The rest of us, who came here to actually work out, are waiting at a polite distance, growing visibly more annoyed, while they remain oblivious or pretend to be.

The squat rack has been occupied for fifty minutes by a man doing curls. Curls. With a barbell that he then unloads and walks away from, leaving the rack tied up while he goes to the water fountain. The rack is for squats. The squats are why the rack exists. There are nine other places in the gym he could be curling. He has chosen the rack because it has a place to lean. I am ready to start a one-man movement to claim the rack by force.

The locker room is overrun with men who insist on having full conversations naked in front of the lockers I need to open. They do not move. They do not pause. They continue blocking the lockers with their wet, unclothed bodies while I attempt to retrieve my belongings without making eye contact with anyone. The communal nudity is fine. The willingness to maintain a conference call atmosphere while being a physical obstruction is not.

Every single treadmill is taken and there is a line of people pretending not to be a line. Each user has set their machine for sixty minutes. The gym has a thirty minute limit posted on signs every twenty feet, which everyone is studiously ignoring. The staff at the front desk are watching this happen and doing nothing. The rule is a fiction. The line is a fiction. The polite veneer of the gym is fraying and I am ready to start enforcing the rules personally.

Someone has stacked all five thousand pounds of plates on a single leg press and left them there. They are not coming back. The plates have been abandoned for fifteen minutes. No one wants to unrack them because no one came to the gym to spend twenty minutes removing one man's vanity weight. The gym has become a graveyard of inconsiderate setups and the rest of us are tip-toeing around the headstones.

The personal trainer has commandeered three machines and the entire stretching area for one client. Three. For one client. The rest of the gym is squeezed into the remaining floor space while a single paying customer enjoys a private studio experience at our expense. The trainer is not even working with the client most of the time. He is on his phone. The client is texting. The machines sit idle while the rest of us circle like vultures.

The man at the cable machine has wrapped a towel around the handle, draped his water bottle on the seat, plugged in his phone, and walked off to use the bathroom for the past ten minutes. The towel claim has been recognized in gym culture as a sacred territorial marker. I do not recognize this culture. I am moving the towel. I am claiming the machine. He can fight me when he returns from his leisurely toilet visit.

The mirrors in front of the dumbbell rack are blocked by an influencer setting up a tripod for a workout video. He is angling the lighting. He is checking the framing. He is doing none of the things one usually does at a dumbbell rack, like lifting dumbbells. The dumbbells I need are behind his ring light. I am asking him to move. He is acting as if this is a hostile request. It is. I am hostile. I have been hostile since I walked in.

There is sweat on the bench. There is sweat on the floor. There is sweat on the handles of the rowing machine. The previous user has left an absolute biological deposit on every surface he touched, and the wipes the gym provides are six aisles away because the dispenser nearest us was emptied three days ago and not refilled. The signs everywhere instruct us to wipe down equipment. The previous user has clearly never read a sign in his life.

Saturday morning at the gym has become a public-square performance of who can be the most inconsiderate. People are doing supersets across half the floor. People are filming themselves in front of the equipment. People are wandering aimlessly between machines, holding them with their hand for no reason, occupying space without using it. The gym has more than enough equipment if everyone used it efficiently. The gym is unusable because no one does.

I have been at the DMV for four hours. The line has moved exactly twelve people. There are nine windows. Two are open. The other seven employees are visibly present, drinking coffee, looking at their phones, having quiet conversations behind partial barriers. The number system has skipped me twice. The kiosk gave me the wrong category of ticket. The supervisor is on break. I have aged in this room. I will leave a different person than I entered.

The application for a permit has been in processing for eleven months. Eleven months. The original estimate was four to six weeks. Every call to check on it produces the same answer, that it is still in processing and there is no further information available. There is a person somewhere who could tell me where my application is. That person is unreachable. There is no email address. There is no extension. There is no recourse. I am simply waiting and being told to keep waiting.

The clerk informed me that the form I filled out was the wrong form, that the correct form is available only at a different building across town, and that the office at that building closes in twenty minutes. She told me this in a tone that suggested I should have known. I did not know. I had no way of knowing. The signage on this building does not mention the other building. The website lists the wrong form. The system is broken and the clerk is enjoying the situation.

The website crashed during the final submission and the form has to be filled out again from the beginning, on a different browser, between the hours of four and six in the morning when fewer users are online. This is the official advice from the department. Wake up at four in the morning to submit your tax extension. The IT department has surrendered. The agency has surrendered. The state has surrendered. The citizens are still expected to perform.

I have spoken to four different government employees about the same issue and received four different answers. None of them are willing to put their answer in writing. None of them will give me a supervisor's name. None of them have any authority to make a decision. The phrase that the system does not allow that is used like a religious incantation, as if the system were a deity with its own will, and not a database administered by people who could change it.

The mail-in renewal arrived three months after I sent it back, with a note that the renewal had been processed but the new card was not enclosed and would arrive in a separate envelope, which has not arrived. The note is the only proof that the renewal happened. The system shows nothing. The phone agents cannot find the record. I am being told to wait six to eight more weeks, which would put me past the expiration date of the very document I renewed.

The benefits office requires an in-person interview. The next available in-person interview is in seventeen weeks. The benefits would have expired four months ago by that date. The office acknowledges this. The office cannot do anything about it. The office suggests reapplying after the lapse, which restarts the clock, and which guarantees I will lose access to the benefits I rely on. This is not bureaucracy. This is institutional cruelty.

The agency lost my paperwork. They lost the original. They lost the copies I sent at their request. They have lost the documentation of having received the copies. They are now asking me to resubmit the entire packet for a third time, certified mail, at my expense, with no guarantee that this time it will be filed correctly. I am paying postage for the privilege of doing the agency's job for them.

The notice arrived in the mail with a deadline that had already passed by the time the envelope was opened. I am being penalized for missing a window I was never made aware of. The postmark proves that the notice was mailed two days before the deadline. There was no possibility of timely response. The fee is non-negotiable. The appeal process requires submitting another form by another deadline, which I now must scramble to meet. This is not a system. This is a maze with consequences.

The clerk read my driver's license number out loud in a busy lobby and then asked me to confirm my social security number at full volume. There is no privacy. There is no security. There is no concern. The clerk has been doing this for years and no one has stopped her, and the people in line can now apply for credit cards in my name if they have a working memory. I am beyond complaint. I am into despair.

He has scheduled a daily check-in meeting that runs forty minutes, during which he asks the same questions in slightly different forms, takes notes I can already see in the project tracker, and concludes with vague encouragement that translates to no actual feedback. I have produced more value in the last hour, after the meeting ended, than during the entire week of meetings that preceded it. The micromanagement has reached parody. I am being managed into uselessness.

Every email I send out is copied to him for approval. Every line of code I push is reviewed line by line by him personally. Every decision I make is overruled, sometimes hours later, in a way that requires me to redo work. He is not a manager. He is a bottleneck with a salary. The team has stopped trying to be efficient because he will undo any efficiency we create. We are paid to do nothing while looking busy.

He requested a status update on a task I started yesterday afternoon. The task is expected to take a week. He wants to know my progress, my obstacles, my next steps, and my projected completion date. He wants this in a spreadsheet, color-coded, with a written narrative attached. The task itself would have been half-finished by now if he had not interrupted me to demand a report on a task I have not had time to do because of the report demands.

He has installed monitoring software on my laptop. It tracks keystrokes, mouse movements, and screen activity. It reports periods of inactivity to his dashboard in real time. I am being surveilled to verify that I am working. I am a senior professional with a decade of experience and he is timing my bathroom breaks. The dignity has not just left the room. The dignity has been chased out with a stick.

He told me to use a different font in the report. He told me which font. He told me which font size. He told me which color the headers should be. He told me the spacing between paragraphs. He told me to use bullet points instead of numbered lists, then ten minutes later told me to use numbered lists instead of bullet points. The content of the report is irrelevant to him. The formatting is the work. I am being paid to be his typesetter.

He called me at nine forty-five on a Friday night to ask about a slide in a deck that is not due until Wednesday. There was no emergency. There was no client request. There was no contextual reason for the call. He was at home, drinking, scrolling through the deck on his phone, and decided he wanted to bother me. The disregard for boundaries is staggering. I am supposed to drop my evening to discuss formatting with a man who cannot leave work at work.

He has rewritten the same paragraph in the proposal seven times. Each rewrite is functionally identical to the last. The differences are word substitutions, comma placements, and the order in which the same three ideas are presented. We are now sixteen hours past the original deadline because of this paragraph. The client has signaled they would have accepted the first version. He cannot let it go. The proposal will never ship because the paragraph will never be perfect.

He wants to be looped in on every decision. Every decision. The decision about which font I just complained about. The decision about which calendar invite color to use. The decision about who orders lunch when the team is in the office. I am no longer empowered to make any decision at all. I have outsourced my judgment to a man whose own judgment is comically poor, and the work product is suffering accordingly.

He has asked me to forward him every email I receive from any client before I respond, so he can approve the response. The volume of emails makes this impossible. He acknowledges this. He has not changed the policy. He simply expects compliance with an unworkable rule and gets quietly furious when responses go out without his blessing. He is angry about the very thing he made impossible. The contradiction is the management style.

He scheduled a one-on-one to discuss why I missed a deadline. The deadline was missed because he asked for revisions to four different pieces of work the day before the deadline, none of which were urgent, all of which took the time I needed to finish the original task. He is now using the missed deadline as evidence that I struggle with time management. The audacity of the framing has rendered me speechless. I have prepared a written rebuttal. It will not change anything.

The ticket was advertised at thirty-nine dollars. At checkout, the price has bloomed to seventy-eight. There is a service fee, a convenience fee, a processing fee, a facility fee, an order processing fee separate from the processing fee, a venue restoration surcharge, and a delivery fee for an electronic ticket that requires no delivery. The base price is a lie. The advertised price is fraud. The whole industry has been engaged in price misrepresentation for years and somehow it is legal.

The hotel charged a resort fee for amenities I did not use, will not use, and was not informed about at booking. The amenities consisted of access to a pool that was closed, a gym that required a separate reservation, and a beach that is public property. The resort fee is thirty-five dollars a night. The total trip cost has expanded by over two hundred dollars. The hotel claims the fee is standard. Standard for what. For whom. By whose authority. The whole concept is a scam wearing a uniform.

The airline ticket included a fee to select a seat. A fee to bring a carry-on. A fee to print the boarding pass at the gate. A fee to check in earlier than two hours before the flight. A fee for early boarding. A fee for water on board. The base fare is now a notional figure that has no relationship to the price I actually pay. The base fare is a recruiting poster. The actual ticket is whatever they decide to extract from you over the course of the booking process.

The rental car was advertised at sixty dollars a day. The final bill is two hundred and forty dollars a day after the airport facility charge, the customer facility fee, the vehicle license recovery fee, the energy recovery fee, the concession recovery fee, the additional driver fee, and three different insurance products that were aggressively up-sold by the counter agent who would not let me finalize the transaction without acknowledging each one. The car is the same car. The destination is the same place. The price is a fiction wrapped in disclaimers.

The phone bill includes a fee for paper billing, a fee for not enrolling in autopay, a regulatory cost recovery fee that is not a tax but resembles one, a federal universal service fee, an administrative fee that is described nowhere in the contract, and a 911 emergency services fee that the carrier appears to keep rather than remit. None of these fees were disclosed when I signed up. All of these fees are non-negotiable.

The restaurant added an automatic gratuity to a party of four, which is two below their stated party-size threshold for automatic gratuity. When questioned, the manager said it was an oversight and could be removed, then deducted only half. The remaining half stayed on the bill as a separate line item with no explanation. I tipped on top of this because I am a coward in restaurant settings, and now I am writing an angry review at home, where bravery is cheap.

The bank charges a monthly maintenance fee for an account I have had for fifteen years, which was originally fee-free. The fee was introduced silently three years ago and has been climbing ever since. The notification of the fee change was buried in a quarterly mailer that looked like junk and was almost certainly thrown away. The bank knows. The bank counts on this. The whole institution is engineered to extract small amounts from inattentive customers in volume.

The concert ticket has now arrived with a delivery fee of seven dollars, in addition to the original five-dollar service fee, and the new emerging-artist support fee, which the venue introduced last year without explaining what an emerging-artist support fee actually supports. The artist on the ticket is not emerging. The artist has been touring for twenty years. The fee is a sleight of hand and the fact that no one has sued over it is the eighth wonder of modern commerce.

The food delivery app advertised free delivery on this order. The total at checkout includes a service fee, a small order fee, a busy area fee, a driver tip suggestion that defaults to twenty-five percent, and a regulatory response fee that I am pretty sure is not regulatory. The free delivery cost thirteen dollars in fees. The food, which was twelve dollars at the restaurant, arrived for thirty-one dollars total. The app is laundering markups through opaque accounting.

The gym contract listed the monthly fee in big bold print and the annual maintenance fee in tiny print at the bottom of page three, where I did not read it. The annual maintenance fee is sixty dollars and arrived as a surprise charge in March. The cancellation requires sixty days' notice in writing, certified mail, to a specific address that is not on the website. The cancellation will not be honored if it does not include the original membership card, which I lost five years ago. The contract is a labyrinth and the gym is the minotaur.

The keyboard autocompleted my message to my mother to suggest she contact emergency services. I had typed are you home and the keyboard, with great confidence, completed it with feeling well or do you need an ambulance. She does not need an ambulance. She needs to know if I should pick up groceries. The autocomplete is performing a comedy routine at my expense and my mother has now called me three times in a panic.

I have typed the word the exactly twelve thousand times this year and the autocomplete still suggests duck every time. Duck. There is no context in which duck is more likely than the. The autocomplete has been trained on a parallel universe in which I run a duck farm and write daily updates about my flock. I have never owned a duck. I have never written about ducks. The phantom duck haunts every message I send.

The email program decided that I meant to address the message to my CEO rather than to my colleague with the same first name. The CEO received my detailed complaint about the broken office coffee machine. The CEO does not handle coffee machines. The CEO now thinks I am the kind of employee who escalates appliance issues to the C-suite. My career may not survive this. The autocomplete has betrayed me utterly.

I am trying to write the word definitely and the autocomplete keeps changing it to defiantly. The two words mean entirely different things. I have corrected this ten times in the last paragraph. The autocomplete has learned, somehow, that I prefer defiantly. I do not prefer defiantly. I have never used defiantly in my life. The autocomplete is rewriting my personality from the bottom up, one word at a time, and I am too tired to stop it.

The search bar is offering me suggestions that have nothing to do with what I am typing. I am typing the name of a town. The suggestions include unrelated products, celebrity gossip, and a question someone else apparently asked last week. The autocomplete is not finishing my thought. The autocomplete is interrupting my thought with someone else's thought. The whole interface is a noisy chaperone preventing me from arriving at the result I came for.

The phone autocompleted my apology into something insulting. I typed I am so sorry and the phone suggested I am so sorry you are like this. I did not see the change before pressing send. The recipient has not responded. The recipient may not respond for a long time. The autocomplete has, in a single act, ended a friendship that took fifteen years to build, and the company that programmed it has a market cap larger than several small nations.

Predictive text just suggested I conclude my work email with kind regrets instead of kind regards. The suggestion is technically grammatical. The suggestion is unhinged. The suggestion came after I had typed kind reg, which is unambiguously the beginning of regards in the context of an email signature. The autocomplete is editorializing. The autocomplete has opinions about my professional relationships. The autocomplete needs to be taken outside and disabled.

I keep accidentally accepting the autocomplete suggestion when I hit space and now my messages contain a phantom selection of words I did not type. Pneumonia. Bordeaux. Antidisestablishmentarianism. These words have appeared in casual texts to my landlord, my sister, my dentist. The recipients are starting to ask if I am okay. I am not okay. The keyboard has assumed creative control over my correspondence.

The dropdown for billing address has me down as living in eleven different cities. The autocomplete has helpfully retained every typo, every old address, every state I have visited and once filled out a hotel form in. There is no way to clear the dropdown. There is no way to edit the list. The list grows every time I shop online. By the time I am eighty, the dropdown will contain my entire residential history and the names of cities I have never set foot in.

I asked the smart assistant to set a timer and it ordered me a pound of timer-related products from a third-party retailer. The order has shipped. I cannot cancel because the assistant placed the order on a payment method I do not recognize, which is apparently linked to my account in a way I never approved. The mystery vendor will appear at my doorstep tomorrow with a box of items I never requested, and the assistant remains cheerful about all of this.

I have filed twelve noise complaints in three months. The neighbors continue to host parties that vibrate the walls until four in the morning. The property manager has spoken to them, as he tells me each time, but the conversations have produced no behavioral change. The police were called twice and responded by knocking once and leaving. The HOA has decided that this falls outside their jurisdiction. Every authority has agreed that the problem is real and that solving it is not their job.

The construction next door starts at six in the morning, six days a week. The city allows construction to begin at seven. The contractor knows this. The contractor does not care. The complaints I file are routed to a portal that says the issue is under review. Under review for what. The crew is here. They are loud. The hours are written on the permit posted on the fence. There is no review necessary. There is enforcement, which no one is doing.

The new bar downstairs has a sound system that shakes the floor of my apartment until two in the morning every weekend. The bar has a permit for music. The permit specifies decibel limits. The bar exceeds those limits routinely. The licensing board has been contacted. The licensing board says it will investigate, which is bureaucratic code for nothing will happen. I am being sonically assaulted on a schedule that the city has effectively approved.

The barking dog has barked continuously for three hours. The owner is not home. The owner has not been home for hours. The owner leaves the dog outside for the entire workday. The animal services line is unstaffed after hours. The non-emergency police line transferred me to animal services. The HOA secretary told me to leave a note on the door. I have left twenty notes. The notes are part of the landscape now. They are weathered and unread.

The leaf blower has been running for ninety consecutive minutes outside my bedroom window. It is Saturday. It is eight in the morning. The decibel level is roughly comparable to a small aircraft. The yard service is contracted by the neighbor. The neighbor is not home. The yard service has no obligation to schedule around my preferences. I am supposed to accept being woken up at the crack of dawn by a gas-powered nightmare as a normal feature of suburban life. I refuse.

The upstairs neighbor stomps. Constantly. Heel-first. Across hardwood floors. At eleven at night. At three in the morning. At five-thirty when she leaves for work. I have asked her to be considerate. I have asked the landlord to intervene. I have considered installing a mirror on the ceiling so I can stare upward at the source of my torment. The landlord shrugs. The neighbor shrugs. The shrugs accumulate into a posture of institutional indifference.

The fireworks have been going off in the neighborhood every night for two weeks. It is not the Fourth of July. It is not a holiday. There is no occasion. The fireworks are illegal in this jurisdiction. The police have been called repeatedly. They have not responded. They have, according to the dispatcher, more pressing concerns. The dogs in the area are traumatized. The veterans in the area are traumatized. The municipality has decided that this is the cost of doing business.

The street parking is now occupied by a truck that idles for thirty minutes every morning while the driver sips coffee. The engine is loud. The exhaust is unmistakable. The driver has been warned by the city. The fine, when issued, is fifty dollars. The truck has paid the fine four times this year. The economics favor continuing the behavior. The fine is now a parking fee. The neighborhood is collateral damage.

The car alarm has been going off for forty minutes. The owner is nowhere to be found. The alarm is doing its job, which is to be unbearable, and is failing its job, which is to summon the owner. The car will continue alarming until someone breaks a window in frustration. The neighborhood is not concerned about the car. The neighborhood is concerned about whoever loses control first and the litigation that may follow.

The motorcycle club has decided that the loop outside my window is their preferred riding route. They come through in groups of twenty, engines modified for maximum volume, late at night, weekly. The route is a public street. The volume is technically within limits because the limits were written before this particular class of exhaust system was invented. The law is from a quieter era. The enforcement is from a fictional one.

Six hours on the tarmac. Six. The pilot keeps providing updates in the same calm voice, each promising imminent departure, each followed by another forty-five minute hold. The catering is gone. The bathrooms are overflowing. The flight attendants have stopped pretending it will be okay. The airline insists that no compensation is owed because of weather, despite the sky being clear. The weather they are blaming is in a different city, two hundred miles away.

The flight has been delayed three times, each by ninety minutes, each communicated five minutes after the previous estimated departure had elapsed. The pattern is now clear. The flight is not delayed. The flight has been canceled in slow motion. The airline is dripping the bad news in small doses to avoid triggering rebooking obligations. The gate agent will not confirm cancellation because the system has not officially canceled. The system is gaslighting an entire terminal.

My flight was canceled and the rebooking algorithm has placed me on a flight three days from now, with a layover in two different cities, on a route that doubles my travel time. The agent at the desk has the authority to do better but will not, citing fare rules. The fare rules are flexible when the airline wants them to be. The fare rules are concrete when I want them to be. The asymmetry is everything that is wrong with this industry.

The boarding sign at the gate has been displaying the boarding time as five minutes ago for the last forty minutes. No boarding has occurred. No announcement has been made. The agents have left the desk. The plane is allegedly at the gate. The passengers are crowded around the jet bridge entrance in a state of nervous shuffling. We are all watching each other for clues. The airline has abandoned us collectively and is hoping we figure something out.

I missed my connection because the first flight was forty minutes late, after which they parked at a remote gate, after which the bus took twenty minutes to arrive, after which they unloaded the elderly first and the wheelchair passengers second and me, in seat 33F, last. By the time I reached the connecting gate it had closed five minutes earlier. The agent there laughed. Actually laughed. And told me to head to customer service to be rebooked, where the line is two hours long.

The airline texted me an apology and a fifty-dollar voucher for a future flight on the same airline. The voucher expires in ninety days, cannot be combined with other offers, cannot be used for taxes and fees, and cannot be used during any blackout date, which appears to be most of the next ninety days. The voucher is an insult disguised as a gesture. I will not be flying this airline again, on principle, and the voucher will expire unused, which is precisely what the airline counted on.

I have been standing in the rebooking line for two hours and fifteen minutes. There are nine people working at the desk and three of them are visibly assisting passengers. The other six are doing something with their computers that does not appear to involve helping the line. The agents who are helping are processing each passenger in twenty-minute increments. The math suggests I will be here past midnight. The flight I was rebooked onto leaves in forty minutes from a different terminal.

The compensation policy states that delays caused by air traffic control are not eligible for refunds. The delay was caused by the airline overbooking the flight and waiting for volunteers to give up their seats. The airline has classified this as an air traffic control delay in its records. The classification is a fiction. The fiction is corporate self-preservation. The customer service team will not respond to the discrepancy and the dispute process requires fifty pages of documentation.

The flight crew has just informed us that they have timed out, that no replacement crew is available, and that the flight is canceled. They are leaving the aircraft. They are walking past us in their uniforms, on their phones, going home. We are still in our seats. We have been in our seats for four hours. We are now expected to deplane, retrieve our luggage, find a hotel, and start over tomorrow. The airline has provided no hotel. The airline has provided no taxi. The airline has provided nothing.

I have just watched the gate agent change my boarding zone from group one to group four with no explanation. The boarding pass on my phone updated automatically. The new boarding zone means I will not get overhead bin space. I will be forced to check my carry-on at the gate. The carry-on contains my laptop, my passport, and my medication. The agent has informed me I can opt to wait and see if there is room. The wait will be ten minutes after the door closes. The flight leaves in fifteen.

I clicked one link to read one article and the site has now spawned three pop-ups, two overlays, a video player that has docked to the bottom of the screen, and a newsletter signup form that covers the bottom half of the article. The article itself is four paragraphs long. The pop-ups are more numerous than the paragraphs. The site has prioritized harvesting my attention over delivering what I came for.

The article cuts off after the first sentence with a wall of subscription options that requires me to either commit to ten dollars a month or close the tab. There is no option to read this single article. There is no option to pay a quarter for the piece. There is only the all-or-nothing wall, designed by someone who fundamentally misunderstands the rhythms of casual reading. I am closing the tab. I am not subscribing. The publisher gets neither my money nor my attention.

The cookie consent banner is so aggressive that it covers the entire page and refuses to dismiss until I have manually deselected sixty-seven different vendor categories. The reject all button is buried two clicks deep, behind a manage settings screen, behind a confirmation, behind a please reconsider dialog. The accept all button is enormous, brightly colored, and clearly meant to be the path of least resistance. The whole UX is engineered to break me.

The newsletter signup overlay just asked me to wait, with a countdown, before I could close it. Wait. With a countdown. For five seconds. The site has decided that my time is worth precisely as little as it can extract by force. I refuse. I close the tab. I delete the link from my history. I will tell anyone who asks that this publication is not worth reading because of the experience of reading it, regardless of the actual content.

The paywall pretends to be a soft paywall, but it tracks my visits across devices, and on the fourth visit the cookie I cleared comes back from the server. The publication has tagged my browser fingerprint. They know it is me. They are showing me a paywall on the third article I have viewed this year. The site is using surveillance infrastructure to enforce a quota I never agreed to. I find this offensive at a level I did not know I could be offended by software.

The popup wants my email. The popup wants my phone number. The popup wants my zip code. The popup wants my age range. The popup wants my income bracket. The popup wants my opinion on three unrelated products. The popup will not close until I provide at least three of these. The popup is a phishing operation dressed up as a subscription form, and the site is hosting it without apology.

The flashlight app wants access to my contacts, my microphone, my location, my calendar, and my photo library. It is a flashlight. It turns on the LED. It does not need to know who my friends are. It does not need to know where I am. It does not need to listen to me. The permission requests are not for the functionality of the flashlight. The permission requests are for the data harvest. The app is a vehicle for surveillance disguised as a utility.

I denied the location permission and the app has stopped functioning. The app does not require location for any of its features. The app does require location for its business model, which is selling my location to data brokers. The app has held its functionality hostage to my permission grant. The choice is now between using the app and giving up information that has no business being part of this transaction. I will uninstall the app. I will leave a one-star review. I will recommend that others do the same.

The game app, an actual children's game, has requested microphone access. To play the game. The microphone is not used in the game. There is no voice interaction. There is no recording feature. The microphone permission is a data acquisition mechanism for the parent company's broader analytics platform. The app is a Trojan horse and the children using it are the targets. The fact that this is legal is one of the great moral failures of the modern app ecosystem.

The app updated and reset its permissions. The location permission, which I had carefully denied, is now on. The microphone permission, which I had explicitly revoked, is now on. The app is now monitoring me again, and the only way to find out was to manually inspect each permission, which the OS does not surface clearly. The trust I had developed with the operating system has eroded. The trust I had developed with the app never existed.

The keyboard app has full access to everything I type. Everything. Passwords, credit card numbers, private messages, search queries. The privacy policy claims this data is used to improve the typing experience, which is corporate doublespeak for sold to the highest bidder. The app I downloaded to get a cute font is the most invasive piece of software on my phone. The trade-off is grotesque, and the fact that we have all accepted it as normal is worse.

The fitness app does not need my contacts. The fitness app should not have my contacts. The fitness app has, somehow, my contacts. It is suggesting that I add friends from my address book to its social platform, which I did not sign up for, and which I do not want. I revoked the contacts permission. The app remembered the contacts anyway, because the data was already uploaded to their servers. The permission revocation is performance. The harvest already happened.

The app demands a permission, then crashes if denied, then prompts again, then crashes again. The cycle continues until I either grant the permission or uninstall. There is no middle path. There is no partial permission. There is no please continue without this feature. The app has been designed as an extortion racket. The app will work only if it gets what it wants. The app is the digital equivalent of someone holding a service hostage until you agree to their terms.

The weather app is reading my SMS messages. The weather. App. Is reading. My text messages. The justification, buried in the privacy policy, is that text messages may contain weather-related information that helps personalize the experience. No one texts me weather. No one has ever texted me weather. The justification is a fig leaf the size of a postage stamp, attempting to cover a permission grab the size of a barn door.

I have spent forty-five minutes auditing the permissions on every app on my phone. The results are devastating. The shopping app can listen to my microphone. The notes app can see my photos. The flashlight app can read my files. The puzzle game can access my health data. The cumulative invasion is total. The phone is no longer a tool. The phone is a surveillance device that occasionally takes calls.

I mentioned, casually, that I had been a little tired lately, and a man I have known for forty-five minutes is now lecturing me about iron supplements, sleep hygiene, screen time, and the failures of modern medicine. I did not ask. I do not want his diagnosis. I want to finish my drink and go home. The unsolicited expertise is louder than the actual conversation. He has confused having strong opinions with being helpful.

My cousin has decided that my career path is wrong, that my apartment is too small, that my partner is unsuitable, that my haircut is unflattering, and that I should consider moving back home. Her own life is a wreck. She has lost two jobs this year. Her landlord is suing her. Her dog is in the news for biting a delivery driver. The audacity of her offering me advice would be funny if it were not aimed at me. I have stopped responding to her texts.

The stranger at the playground has informed me that my child is dressed too warmly, that I am holding her wrong, that the snack I gave her is not nutritious, and that her shoe is on the incorrect foot. The shoe is on the correct foot. I checked. I am holding my child. I have been holding her for three years. The stranger is a retired teacher, which she has mentioned twice in the first minute, and the credential has apparently licensed her to deliver parenting reviews unsolicited.

I posted a photo of my new garden and three strangers in the comments have informed me that the soil is the wrong pH, that the spacing is incorrect, that the plant choices are unsustainable, and that I should consider native species, the wisdom of permaculture, and a particular YouTube channel that will, they assure me, change my life. I did not ask for the YouTube channel. I do not want the lecture. I am happy with the garden. The internet has decided otherwise.

The coworker who has been at the company for three months is now explaining the project to me. To me. The person who built it. He has read the documentation, which I wrote, and has helpful corrections about how I have structured the work. He is delivering these corrections as advice, in a friendly tone, as if I will be grateful. I am not grateful. I am furious that I have to smile and nod while he repackages my own ideas back to me as wisdom.

The acquaintance at the dinner party has decided that I would benefit from her unsolicited wisdom on my dating life, my financial decisions, my exercise habits, and my food choices, despite the fact that I have not asked for any of this and have given no indication of welcoming the feedback. She has positioned herself as a guru. She is a real estate agent. The advice is generic, dated, and faintly insulting. I am counting the minutes until I can excuse myself.

I mentioned that I had been to the doctor and the response was a forty-minute tangent about essential oils, the failures of allopathic medicine, the dangers of vaccines, and the curative properties of a tea sold by a multi-level marketing company my acquaintance has just joined. I did not ask. I do not want the tea. I do not want the lecture. I want to finish my coffee. The unsolicited advice has crossed from annoying into actively dangerous and I am leaving this brunch.

The neighbor has stopped by, again, to suggest improvements to my landscaping. He has thoughts on the tree placement. He has thoughts on the mulch choice. He has thoughts on the bird feeder. He has thoughts on the color of the front door. His own yard is a chaos of unmown grass and abandoned lawn furniture. The brazen disconnect between his expertise and his execution is breathtaking. I have stopped opening the door when I see him approaching.

The relative who has never run a business is explaining to me how to run my business. He is providing advice based on a podcast he listened to last week and a book he read part of in 2018. He is delivering it with the certainty of a CEO. The advice is wrong. Some of it is illegal. The rest is impractical. I have tried to redirect the conversation three times. He will not be redirected. He has come prepared with talking points.

The stranger on the train has just informed me that my book is overrated, that the author is problematic, and that I should be reading something else entirely. He did not ask what I think of the book. He did not introduce himself. He simply opened the conversation with a critique of my reading material as if I had requested a review. I am putting on headphones. I am turning to the window. I am, for the rest of this train ride, a wall.

I have not asked for your opinion. I have not asked for your guidance. I have not asked for your wisdom. I have not asked for your story about how you went through something similar twenty years ago and learned the following lesson. I am venting. The appropriate response to venting is a brief expression of sympathy, not a lecture. The fact that I have to explain this to a grown adult is itself a small tragedy.

Twelve dollars for a hot dog that tastes like cardboard wrapped around regret and they have the audacity to charge a service fee. Everyone behind this counter should be ashamed of themselves. The entire concept of stadium food pricing is a scam designed by people who clearly hate their customers.
